is always room for improvement.

report on YWCA camps; Ted Yard 
for a release on his Western trip. 

And we welcome with rousing cheers 
yet another new member, The Alberta 
Camping Association. This is a clear 
indication of an increased camping 
interest in that prairie province, and 
we are encouraged by such progress. 
May it grow in stature and numbers, 
and may we enjoy association with its 
members for many years to come.

From 


the President 5 s Desk 


Westward tto! 

We camping people have each found 
at one time or another that by visiting 
camps other than our own we inevitably 
receive stimulation and inspiration. By 
this token, your President’s cup was 
certainly filled to overflowing during 
this year of 1953. 

During the course of the year, we 
have had the privilege of visiting Camps 
Kitchikewana, Glen Bernard, Gay Ven¬ 
ture, Bark Lake, Norval, Onawaw, Sun- 
fish and Boulderwood in Ontario. In 
most instances we were able to see these 
camps in operation, and then when 
most of our campers had left for home, 
we started on a camping trip which was 
to take us through over 8,000 miles of 
driving into many camps in our west¬ 
ern provinces and some in the United 
States. 

In Manitoba, in addition to visiting 
several camps and learning at first hand 
about the unique day camp sites the 
city of Winnipeg makes available to the 
various agencies, we had the privilege 
of meeting with the Camping Associa¬ 
tion Executive and members, and of 
addressing a special meeting where 
Camp Directors, staff people, parents 
and campers were all present. As 
always, it was a pleasure to meet with 
our Canadian Camping Vice-President, 
Mrs. MacDonald and with Miss Eliza¬ 
beth Connall, President of the Mani¬ 
toba Camping Association and her 
energetic Executive Committee. 

In Saskatchewan we visited several 
centres although, at the moment, the 
C.C.A. does not have a section in this 


province. We learned there are a great 
number of camps operated through the 
Church organizations and through the 
Scouts and, in addition, we had an 
opportunity to meet the staff and lay 
people responsible for the operation of 
the Y.M.C.A. camps in Regina and 
Saskatoon. 

At Calgary we met representatives 
from the various Church organizations 
which are operating camps, and also 
from the Boy Scouts, Girl Guides, 
Y.M.C.A. and Salvation Army. To this 
meeting, camping enthusiasts flew 
several hundred miles from Edmonton, 
and drove north a considerable distance 
from Lethbridge. In a spirit of genuine 
co-operation, camp people from these 
three large centres drew together their 
camping interests and decided to form 
the Alberta Camping Association, with 
Mr. Murray Faulkner of the Calgary 
Y.M.C.A., as the acting President of 
the group. 

In Banff we had consultations with 
a gentleman who is keenly interested 
in establishing a private camp for boys 
in this beautiful national park, and in 
the Okanagan Valley we had an oppor¬ 
tunity to see several of the B.C. camp¬ 
sites. 

In Vancouver, it was your President’s 
privilege to address 60 members and 
friends of the B.C. Camping Associa¬ 
tion and also, on another occasion, to 
tneet with Charles Roche, the energetic 
President of that Association, and mem¬ 
bers of his Executive . It was a pleasure 
also to speak to Third and Fourth year

— - • : to Ontario (again through 
—r^zhkn Provinces), we arrived 

in time to attend Major 

- hoard meeting of the Ontario 
-- A*ociation and to learn that 

w Association Miss Ruby 


Smith, Miss Nan Vail, Mrs. Agnes 
Mutchler, Mr. Ken Murray and Miss 
Dais Gass, who have given devoted 
leadership to our Association in that 
beautiful province for many years, have 
again assumed active executive roles. 

One cannot complete a trip such as 
ours without recognizing again and 
again the immensity of our country and 
the tremendous task that faces any 
National organization. We are fortunate 
indeed that our Association members 
are almost exclusively “purpose mem¬ 
bers” who join with us in an effort to 
accomplish something far beyond the 
reach of their own individual camp 
operation. I was impressed over and 
over again by the truly purposeful, 
consecrated nature of our membership 
and we could not help but feel that 
despite geography and the barriers of 
mountains and plains, the Canadian 
camping people have indeed a National 
Association. 

MAY WE INTRODUCE . . . 

It is our pleasure to introduce, at 
this time, Mrs. Eanswythe Flynn^ the 
Executive Secretary of our Camping 
Association and Editor of the Canadian 
Camping Magazine. Mrs. Flynn brings 
to our Association a keen and active 
interest in organized camping, and to 
the magazine, experience and skills 
which I am sure we will all come to 
appreciate. Please feel free to write to 
Mrs. Flynn at the Camping Association 
office, 236 Bloor Street W., Toronto, 
with regard to Association matters or 
to editorial content for the Canadian 
Camping magazine. 

W. E. (Ted) Yard 


wmada, December , 1953

Towards A Philosophy 


John Hoyle 

Director , Camp GayVenture 
President , Ontario Camping Association 


Discipline is part of the warp and 
woof of adequate human behaviour. It 
is an essential part of family life, school 
life, military life and of all business 
relationships. No grouping of people, 
adults or children, can function effect¬ 
ively without discipline. Certainly no 
camp can accomplish its objectives 
without a satisfactory form of discipline. 

When, however, we begin to consider 
discipline more carefully, we find a very 
great variance in its purpose, its method 
and its application. Perhaps the place 
to start is to define the meaning of 
discipline. A study of definitions as 
given in several generally accepted 
dictionaries furnish a variety of mean¬ 
ings to the word—perhaps as many 
variations in terminology as there 
appears to be in its practice. One set 
of meanings indicates that discipline 
is a method of securing and maintain¬ 
ing order according to some prescribed 
system of rules; it is a control gained 
by enforcing obedience or order; it 
involves instruction and punishment. 

This approach to discipline suggests 
that discipline is something super-im¬ 
posed upon campers, in order that 
they may behave in accordance with 
the requirements of the Director or 
supervising committee. No doubt this 
form of discipline gets results—certain 
types of results—because the campers 
do what they are told. They are 


flO 


of Camping _r 


coerced by fear of consequences to 
behave in a certain way; they then 
become automata controlled by 
external compulsion. 

Discipline is obviously necessary be¬ 
cause if campers were allowed to do as 
they please, they would soon become a 
problem to their camp, their home and 
their school. However, while this ex¬ 
terior and enforced pressure may suc¬ 
ceed in changing outward behaviour, 
what is it doing to the child? Unless 
the camper accepts this form of be¬ 
haviour voluntarily, so that his inner 
thoughts and emotions are in harmony 
with the controls, little, if any, real 
progress in self-controlled behaviour is 
being achieved. 

If one looks at the root of the word 
discipline, it is quickly ascertained that 
the above concept of discipline is far 
removed from its original meaning. In 
the original Latin the word was 
DISCIPULUS—a follower; the French 
adaptation was DISCERE—to learn. 
While many great leaders of the past 
have had their disciples, it is easiest for 
us to take the outstanding example of 
Jesus Christ and His disciples. What 
type of control did He exercise over 
them? Certainly, it was not the type 
of pressure referred to above. Was it 
not rather a relationship, a sharing of 
life, a mutual understanding and re¬ 
spect resulting in a fprm of behaviour 


Canadian Camping 



m - \ ..tied by the desire of the disciples 
v : .ction in a way set forth, and 
Itory to their unique Teacher. It 
h- ±- contention of the writer that this 

.. is the one most truly related 

li cat form of behaviour that we refer 
| as diKipline. Unless there is a 
— - >saJ relationship between the one 

.5 the leadership and those 
. .. the resulting behaviour is 
-operficial. In the case of the 
Teacher, He motivated His dis- 
50 that they desired above all 
' conduct themselves according 
. Alandard of behaviour which He 
pra i i ited. In other words, life in 
it- snail, but world-shaking group 
^ * ay of living happily and effect- 
ji harmony with the objectives 
^ v - Great Teacher. 


Iftzi we then suggest that essentially 
■is simply “A way of living 
- together in accordance with 
v rJef*.—not primarily because of 
T " n r compulsion, but because the 
- r- understand that if they desire 
pe* happily and healthily together 
cceptance of and conformity to 
rales are essential. 


Interesting in this connection 
ec the definition of discipline as 
the Division of Mental Health 
Department of National Health 
‘felfare, Ottawa. “Discipline is 
[ n child so that he learns to get 
• lith his family, his friends and 
leaching him to behave in an 
way.” 

we need to spend more time 
bf mie campers to understand the 
of each rule and thus secure 
:|Bcal, mental and emotional 
to those controls which ex- 
Has indicated are essential to 
- _ element of a happy and healthy 
One doesn’t have to compel 
to step into a disinfectant 


before and after bathing, because they 
understand it is for their own personal 
hygiene and that of the camp. Campers 
gladly co-operate in rinsing their hands 
in a disinfectant after visiting the “jons” 
for the same reason. When children 
understand through patient explanation 
of the rules of camp, there is no diffi¬ 
culty as regards discipline. 

The good old rule of satisfaction 
applies here as in every form of camp 
behaviour. If the camper understands 
that every rule in camp is for his and 
his fellows’ own health and happiness 
and that compliance with these rules 
bring about satisfaction, then he gladly 
continues to practise that type of be¬ 
haviour. It would appear that one of 
the chief reasons why camps sometimes 
have disciplinary problems is due to the 
authorities not taking the campers into 
their confidence and helping them to 
understand the “why” of each regula¬ 
tion. 

But there is more than this to camp 
discipline. Discipline is essentially the 
function of the cabin counsellors; 
whether discipline is present or other¬ 
wise depends primarily on him or on 
her. Granted the Director is the final 
incarnation of camp discipline, it is 
nevertheless the cabin counsellor who 
is on the firing line twenty-four hours 
a day, and the emergence of a well- 
disciplined camp depends upon him or 
her. He it is who has the responsibility 
of interpreting the theory of discipline 
into the constructive, social and indi¬ 
vidual behaviour of each member of 
his cabin group. 

The writer would like to suggest five 
basic requirements for the attainment 
of the type of discipline which he has 
been discussing. 

I. Effective discipline grows out of love 
and understanding. These are basic. 


Canada , December , 1953 


11 





The counsellor must truly* deeply and 
sincerely love his campers if he is to 
achieve discipline. Love and under¬ 
standing are not synonymous. A 
counsellor may love his campers with¬ 
out understanding them, and he may 
understand his campers technically 
without loving them. Human person¬ 
ality is so constituted that love is 
essential to growth and progress* and 
there can be no growth and progress 
without understanding. 

II. The type of love of which we are 
speaking is not just sentimental love, 
but love that is deeply tinged with 
respect for human personality. This 
love and understanding must be en¬ 
riched and backed up by a calm, quiet 
firmness which inculcates respect and 
gives the campers that sense of security 
in their leadership, without which no 
discipline can be effective. What a 
marvellous combination—love, under¬ 
standing, respect. 

III. Adequate discipline, strange to 
relate because at first they seem contra¬ 
dictory, is the ability of the counsellor 
to identify himself with his cabin group. 
So long as the counsellor remains 
separate from and above his group, he 
will have problems of behaviour. As 
he increasingly identifies himself with 
the group, his problems will tend to 
disappear. Identification is only pos¬ 
sible, of course, to the counsellor who 
loves and is loved, because only such a 
counsellor will be respected for what he 
is, not just for his rank as a staff 
member. The counsellor who earns the 
respect of his group will have no be¬ 
haviour or disciplinary problems, except 
in the case of the occasional child who 
is a nonconformist and must be handled 
in a different way. 

IV. Just as campers respond to affec¬ 
tion and to understanding, so they 


respond to a firm hand. Campers 
definitely do not respond to a sloppy 
counsellor who doesn’t know what he 
is doing or why. They do, however, 
quietly respect the counsellor who 
understands his job and so leads his 
cabin group, that each one takes his 
share of duties, interests and activities. 
Campers learn only too soon if the 
effervescence of the counsellor is just 
skin deep. One cannot bluff campers 
for long. On the other hand, the 
counsellor who has earned their respect 
because of his quiet firmness and 
insistence on duties being properly 
carried out will find himself in an 
invulnerable position. 

V. Possibly the most vital factor in 
discipline is the example the counsellor 
sets to his group and to the camp at 
large. One of our Section Heads this 
summer in making her bi-monthly 
report on the C.I.T.s attached to her 
Section said, “C.I.T.’s need to remem¬ 
ber that campers are watching them 
when off duty, as well as when they 
are on duty.” How easy it is to keep 
keyed up while in charge of an activity 
or a cabin group, and then to let up 
when the assigned duty is completed. 
The counsellor may let up, but the keen 
eyes and ears of the campers are always 
on the alert. The old maxim “that 
what you are speaks so loudly that we 
cannot hear what you say” is as true 
to-day as ever. We who accept the 
great responsibility of cabin counselling 
are really “on show” all the time. 
Counselling is really a twenty-four hour 
a day job. Of course it’s tough, but 
what job really worth doing is not 
tough? To be a cabin counsellor is one 
of the greatest privileges given to young 
men and women, and the responsibili¬ 
ties that accompany it are very great. 
But it’s worth it, isn’t it?

Canadian Camping 


o Lean Years 


Lie Ahead? 

F. Klein 

Professor of Social Work , University of Toronto 


* . kd not travelled very far when 
came upon a vast area without 
The soil was sandy and 
covered with grassy patches, 
me results of erosion were every- 
a> be seen. This had once been 
r'^rm land, but now the top soil 
^ and drought, a constant corn- 
rendered it useless. 

He were told that this was the result 
^providence. Timber had been 
cut without regard to the 
of nature, and the lands that 
retained their life-giving moisture 
. in dust. It was the result of 
£ ithout giving, of cutting with- 
. 'anting. There is an inexorable 
of nature: that one cannot farm 
- endlessly without planting 

and replenishing the soil. For 
v-ho do, there are lean years 


Arrf so. for years we have been ac- 
the bounty of our communities 
takim our crop of counsellors with- 
teeard for the need to plant and 
in order to reap. As a result, 
in lie ahead. Every year it 
e more difficult to get a full staff. 
Hc-e camps each year the average 
of counsellors is growing younger, 
once they attracted University 
:> graduates and teachers, they 
"i ' high school students. The crop 
p _r ellors has not been cultivated; 
t xb! has not been enriched; there 


are rows to hoe and work to do. For, 
if we do not, then lean years may lie 
ahead. 

It should be obvious that nothing is 
gained by camp directors competing for 
the diminishing supply of staff. Forcing 
salary levels up is not the solution. 
It is equally clear that we cannot sit 
back and moan that people have no 
sense of responsibility and that youth, 
today, has lost its soul. Whether you 
agree that we are reaping the result 
of our own improvidence for failing 
to raise our own crop of counsellors out 
of our camps, or for failing to interpret 
our work to the community, or you 
disagree . . . the time has come for all 
camp people to work together to in¬ 
crease the available yield of staff and 
the quality of the crop. 

Some Steps that Might be Taken: 

To Enrich the Soil— 

1. A campaign to acquaint parents 
with the values of counselling to the 
counsellor. 

2. Wholesale interpretation to or¬ 
ganizations; i.e.—Home and School, 
Women’s Institutes, Service Clubs, etc. 
of the leadership training that counsel¬ 
ling produces. 

3. More and better films interpreting 
camping. 

4. Increased lay participation on 
camp committees of individual camps^ 
as well as camping associations. 


Canada , December , 1953 


13 


5. Increased publicity and public 
relations in the press and other media. 

To Improve the Crop— 

1. Better interpretation and forma¬ 
lized channels for developing counsel¬ 
lors out of campers. 

2. Direct appeals for counsellors in 
periodicals that teen-agers read, and 
by speeches and films in schools and 
youth organizations. 

3. Far better counsellor-in-training 
programmes. 

4. Support for the provincial coun¬ 
sellor training efforts. 

5. Year-round follow-up on counsel¬ 
lor recruiting, get-togethers, clubs, etc. 

6. Developing camp clubs on the 
University campus. 

7. Direct interpretation to teachers, 
clergy and vocational guidance person¬ 
nel. 


8. Winter camp during winter vaca¬ 
tion (or counsellor training on a co¬ 
operative basis). 

9. Better interpretations to and 
supervision of counsellors on the job. 

10. Talk camping and sell camping 
. . . not just your camp. 

There are, doubtless, many other 
ways to tackle the job. There is no 
one way. Either we let the thing go to 
dust, for the top soil is about gone, and 
we are now having to dig for staff, or 
we enter into cut-throat competition for 
available staff, with the inevitable evil 
results; or we get together on a co¬ 
operative basis. The latter means 
planting the seed, cultivating the soil 
(parents and other adults); it means 
developing a constant supply of quality 
counsellors. 

If we do not, lean years may lie 
ahead.

wows were held of old. On this rock 
is carved an inscription to “Old Walt”, 
for Walt Whitman spent much time in 
this area which he loved. 

Back to Kaladar, where we took the 
King’s Highway west to Fenelon Falls 
and CAMP KAGAWONG. We were 
pleased to visit here with Bill Chap¬ 
man, for we had known his father for 
many years. As we went about camp 
we sensed that all is well at KAGA¬ 
WONG under Bill’s direction. Thence 
to the Lake Simcoe area, where we 
made our first visit to camp by boat—- 
CAMP SHAWANAGA, at Port Severn 
on Georgian Bay, and met the Hart¬ 
mans. We were delighted with a new 
type of camp architecture in the studio 
for arts and crafts designed by the 
directors. Uniquely this camp oper¬ 
ates the first-month session for junior 
girls, the second month for teen age 
girls.

Earlier, we referred to more than 
twenty-five summers in which we had 
visited camps in some good camping 
area while in operation. The question 
may arise in your minds, how, on a 
brief visit, we really get a true picture 
of the camp in operation. If ydu take 
two months per year out of twenty-five, 
the total would be more than fifty 
months which, if divided into years, 
figures more than four years. We inject 
this figure, for it is evident that after 
spending so much time with directors at 
the base of their activities, one develops 
almost a sixth sense. As you walk about 
a camp with the director or a staff 
member, much is seen and recognized 
about which words are never spoken. 
And so we come to a critical moment. 
We cannot say that camp procedures 
in all of the Ontario camps which we 
visited meet even the minimum stand¬ 
ards of the Canadian Camping Associa¬ 
tion or our own Association. We are 
aware of the efforts that are being made 
to raise the standards of camping in 
your country and ours and we also are 
aware of the many difficulties involved 
—not only for the Association but for, 
the individual camp director. In some 
instances we found too relaxed pro¬ 
gramming; in others over rigidity; but 
we found these in but a few places. 
We recognized in a few camps that 
some counsellors were^ too young in 
actual years and again we realize the’ 
difficulty in securing qualified counsel¬ 
lors of the age required by minimum 
standards. In several cases camp equip¬ 
ment was not adequately kept and 
property not as attractive as it could 


I rmto, Canada, December, 1953 


17 



be without too much additional effort. 
Yes! in a few instances there were 
discontented faces:—not only among 
campers but also staff, which reflects 
upon top direction. Actually, had we 
visited the same number of camps in 
an area in our own country which we 
had not previously visited, our experi¬ 
ence would have been very similar. 

Over and over during those five 
weeks in Ontario we were asked what 
impressed us most about Canadian 
camps. If we choose but one of the 
many impressions it is your tripping 
programs. The pre-training, the prep¬ 
aration, the tripping equipment, the 
skilled leadership, your lakes and 
streams, your tripping. We are im¬ 
pressed with the training, the know¬ 
how of living in the open which you 
give to your campers. We are im¬ 
pressed with the lack of over stimula¬ 
tion, with the naturalness and flexi¬ 
bility of program, with your apprecia¬ 
tion that the camp situation is a 
laboratory where children most easily 
learn the skills and techniques of group 
living. But above all and beyond, it 
is the people we met—the directors and 
staff members—who made a lasting 
impression on us. Words are inade¬ 
quate to express our appreciation of 
the welcome we received and the hospi¬ 


tality extended to us. If we were 
limited to a word with which to 
describe Canadian Camp Directors, 
that word needs must be “warm¬ 
hearted.” Perhaps this is the key to 
the character of the people who have 
so ably developed camping for children 
in Ontario. 

On the lighter side, we shall remem¬ 
ber—the trip to TANAMAKOON 
between the beds of water lillies—the 
way hot baths are taken on the cabin 
docks at MAZINAW—Bill Chapman’s 
art at KAGAWONG—Mr. Norton’s 
red wool shirt at PATHFINDER—the 
spitting ring for teeth-cleaning at GAY- 
VENTURE — the twelve-foot canoes 
for juniors at KANDALORE — the 
council ring over the lake at TAMAK- 
WA—the fairy glen at GLEN BERN¬ 
ARD—the canoe counsellors’paddling 
exhibition at AROWHON—the Cam- 
boose at SHERWOOD FOREST—the 
evening fishing trip at WABI-KON, 
and the talk of old times and old 
friends at AHMEK and WAPOMEO. 
We’ll remember the days in the “Bush” 
—the two-piece bathrooms—the beauti¬ 
ful lakes—the excellent highways—that 
vye “slept in” not “slept late”—but 
most of all we’ll remember the splendid, 
gallant people with whom we spent 
those five weeks in Ontario in 1953.

pa answers, and Mary Barker was 
reefed. 

'Tt had to be done, so we simply 
le time for it,” this busy executive 
as we talked to her about the pro- 
Actually, from the standpoint of 
less and the time element, this was 
the year to leave her desk. As 
:tor of Health and Physical Educa- 
for the YWCA of Canada, Miss 
arker can become more than a little 
in a multitude of details. To 
that, the National Convention in 
provided her with enough extra 
to keep her early summer days 
thing but dull. Yet, if she were to 
such a report at all, it was 
Essary to see the camps in action. 



in YWCA Camps 


Barker’s summer schedule. Her report 
was to be detailed, but not an inspection 
made with a critical eye. Rather it was 
to take the form of a series of friendly 
visits for the purpose of jotting down 
statistics and taking pictues. She was 
to commandeer a photographer and be 
on her merry way. 

They travelled by car, one camp to 
each trip. Over a six-week period, 
seven camps in Ontario and two in 
Quebec provided the necessary informa¬ 
tion and made possible an eight-milli¬ 
metre movie which, now edited by Miss 
B., takes forty minutes to run, and is 
available to anyone who would like to 
borrow it . . . for free. 

“Now, please don’t give anyone the 
impression that this is a glamour 
movie,” she urged modestly. “There’s 
nothing Hollywood about it. In fact, 
I’m afraid our need for the strictly 
practical shocked my photographer 
friend’s sense of the artistic. We took 
these pictures purely to show actual 
facilities in use. It could be called a 
Documentary, for we did it as a guide 
for other camp directors who are build¬ 
ing and require on-the-spot informa¬ 
tion”. 


S , a series of conferences resulted 
b die decision that a tour of YWCA 
l ips became a “piority” in Miss 


To examine the three broad sheets 
of Miss Barker’s report is to know that 
in camps whose areas cover from five 


f onto, Canada, December, 1953 


19 




acres to six hundred acres, groups 
numbering from forty-two to one hun¬ 
dred and fifty campers age eight to six¬ 
teen were housed, or tented, or both, 
at a cost per week ranging from $14.00 
to $20.00 Their camping period 
averaged two weeks and in most cases 
medical examinations were required. 

Except for key people, staff consisted 
of unpaid counsellors in the fifteen to 
thifty-five age group, assisted by C.I.T.’s 
from thirteen to seventeen years of age. 
All camps included a resident registered 
nurse, a doctor on call, cooks, kitchen 
assistants and maintenance man. 

Facilties differed, of course, from 
camp to camp, according to the district, 
to the amount of community interest 
and to the individual donations made 
in each case. But, by and large, they 
could take care of programmes to in¬ 
clude swimming, life saving, canoeing, 
rowing, nature, hiking, overland and 
water tripping, archery, campcraft, 
dramatics, stars and weather, fishing, 
handicraft, music and dancing. Boats 
were in excellent condition, she told us, 
although one camp might have less than 
half-a-dozen craft,"where one in 
particular was proud-as-punch of its 
twenty-five canoes and extensive water¬ 
front programme. 

Buildings came in all manner of 
shapes and sizes, the very modem 
designs in striking contrast to those of 
the “pioneer” variety. Few camps were 
without craftshop , recreation lodge, 
chapel, administration building, dining 
hall, infirmary; most could include as 
well, a nature cabin, campcraft hut, 
counsellor’s recreation hut and boat 
house. 

:While some YWCA camp washing 
facilities are primitive, all but one have 


cold running water, none has hot. One 
camp has cold showers, but all have 
both hot and cold running water in the 
kitchens. Three camps know the j6ys 
of dishwashing machines, four cook 
with electricity, the rest with coal or 
wood, propane gas or natural gas, and 
most have electric refrigeration. 

Fly control is a must with YWCA' 
camp directors, and DDT is the most 
widely used purge; however, those who 
have tried out the Big Stinky wouldn’t 
have anything else. Sanitary facilities 
can be primitive, but»a good many 
camps combine the out-house model 
with chemical, pail-a-day or flush 
toilets. 

Waterfront equipment was most 
satisfactory, docks built in the H, T, I 
or X shape or the Red Gross design. 
Five camps had provided lifeguard 
towers, all used ring bouys, eight owned 
water patrol boats and eight provided 
rafts. 

Curious to know what particular im¬ 
pressions this experience had made on 
Miss Barker, we put the question. Here 
is the substance of her reply: 

“The water craft situation . . . also 
the food . . . was very much better than 
I’d anticipated. So often the supply 
and condition of boats and canoes is 
inadequate to properly serve the num¬ 
ber of campers. 

“Then I was pleased to find no over¬ 
crowding. One camp in particular, 
which, in its ‘private’ days had packed 
in 120 campers, now held its normal 
capacity of sixty. 

“Altogether I have high hopes for 
the future of camping in the Canadian 
YWCA.”

To sit back and remember camping 
tr recall the many pleasant aspects of 
recent Maritime visit. Remember, 
bit of writing is without malice, 
: when I say something like “the 
down east”, or “the fellows in 
Canada”, etc., etc., it’s just a 
ner of speaking and that’s all, but 
I wanted to say was that when 
talk Camp in the Maritimes, you 
informed in a nice way, that the 
camps in Canada are down that-a- 
It was even uttered in more salty 
such as: “Best dum camps”, if 
^13 pardon the expression; “the place 
camping is camping”, and so on. 
aps those Nova Scotians are right, 
m have to admit that when I flew 
Yarmouth to Halifax I couldn’t 
a country could be threaded 
so many thousands of lakes, and of 
the ocean is marged with miles 
fling white sand beach. What 
i could one ask? 


W dl, the point is that from the camp 
point of view, there are many 
cally beautiful, well-located YM 
in that part of the world. Natur- 
one finds the odd one that would 
to move to a more camp-like 
a, but by and large, the Maritime 
are attractive spots. 

Ii was music to the ears to hear 
like Naskapie, Pascobac, Wapo- 
and Barachois, for they conjure up 


all sorts of exciting thoughts about 
“Injuns” and stuff. Bert Messacar’s 
Camp Magaguadavic is pronounced 
“Maggie-Davie” and conjures up in my 
mind the terrible time I used to have in 
Spelling back in school days. Here, 
though, we have a picturesque, natural 
camp setting with a great expanse of 
canoeing country, a chain of lakes and 
natural portages comparable to the best 
in any part of Canada. 

Big Cove reminds me a bit of Pine- 
crest, only it sits in a cove on the ocean. 
So does Holland Cove, and both make 
you think of the times that the Pirate 
Captains dropped off and buried their 
loot in the beach. They really did, too! 
Here ocean swimming’s at its best. A1 
Tyler’s “Y’s Acres” of Moncton, situ¬ 
ated on the Bay of Fundy, with its high 
tide, and the Sherbrooke Camp in one 
of the most colourful parts of Quebec’s 
Eastern Townships, both hold a spell 
over campers and staff alike. 

I must admit that the Saint John 
“Pascobac” threw me for a while, as I 
thought it was Montagnais for “Pass 
the Picobac”. But Myles Dewar and his 
boys soon put me straight. So, along 
with my broken nose, I shall always 
remember that it isn’t what I thought it 
was. Some day I’m going to ask him 
what it does mean! 

Now for a rundown . . . it’s Naskapie 
of Quebec City, Pascobac of Str John,

Let's talk it over 


HAROLD H. THOMPSON 

Building Contractor 
Gravenhurst Ontario 


so on. He started it in answer to the 
problem of constantly changing camp 
directors, particularly in Agency Camps, 
and organized it as a manual divided 
into four sections: Programme, Admin¬ 
istration, Buildings and Equipment. In 
looseleaf form, information can be 
added as situations must be coped with, 
so that every policy is recorded over the 
years. If it became necessary that a 
new director take over either of his 
camps next week, the “inner workings” 
of organization is down on paper, in 
black and white, for him to follow. 

Someone back home asked me how 
“those fellows Down East” cope with 
water safety in ocean camps. Actually, 
their problems do differ a bit from ours 
in that the tide affects waterfront 
activities, and equipment must be built 
to allow for it. The principle of their 
docks in Cove camping is a permanent 
structure on the beach, the actual dock 
and diving towers a long way out (in 
deep water) and built on drums to 
allow for the swell. Swimming areas 
are marked off with floating bouys, the 
anchor chains of which are left slack to 
permit maximum rise and fall. 

As far as programme is concerned, 
it is very much like that in Ontario. 
Hiking and climbing offer many joys; 
rowing, swimming and sailing are 
geared to the ocean’s whims. And when 
you ask a director how far one is 
allowed to sail, the usual reply is: * 
“Well, Ireland is out-of-bounds!” 

I’m all for a spell of this Nova Scotia 
camping; Fd like to catch my own 
lobsters and crabs, bake them and eat 
them with the roar of the surf in my 
ears. So maybe I’ll pack my bedroll 
and haversack, come some sunny sum¬ 
mer Sunday, and strike out for that 
famed “playground of Canada”.

AS CAMP SHOULD BE 
to a First Year Counsellor 

Nfaybe I expected too much of camp, 
a= i therefore should not be writing 

- * fit it at all. But, on the other hand, 
-1 companions who also experienced 
hr it first summer as camp counsellors 

the same as I do. Something was 
-dting, perhaps, or it could be that 
emphasis was, in some cases, in the 
'long place. 

Was it my lack of perception? Or 
■* my director at fault? 

That I have yet to find out. I do 
that all through the winter, camp 
od before me as a golden Utopia 
inne I would find relaxation and 
-jeace as I learned from older counsel- 
-xm* and my director the true concept 
leadership and all that goes with it. 

- expected to come through this ex- 
■-lienee having developed a philosophy 

‘aids camping that would stand by 
m for years to come. So far, I’m still 

- the dark. 

What is wrong with camp in the eyes 
young counsellors, you ask? 

Mainly, not enough training. Yes, 
can hear you. There are Counsellor 
nuning Courses in the spring. Every 
offers some sort of pre-camp 
tduction. But there it stops. What do 
** g** as camp progresses? A staff 
meeting every day in which we go over 
^ogramme, plan the camp’s big event 
the year and talk about getting to 
*> d early every night. We might have 
• • odd get-together with the Section 
Head. 


But to us who are eighteen-going-on- 
nineteen, a continual in-camp training 
plan is a necessity. We are told before¬ 
hand that children must be handled 
with diplomacy, that we should get to 
know them, that we should bring out 
the best in them, that we should be 
able to walk into our respective tents 
and talk freely with our groups. That’s 
all right for someone who is an old 
hand at the game. But how do we 
bring out the best in a child whose 
conception of good camping is to balk 
at everything the counsellor suggests? 
What are the best steps to take in 
getting to know strange children who 
are often painfully shy? What does one 
say? 

We agree . . . the one great point 
about camping is that it gives a counsel¬ 
lor an opportunity to deal with his 
campers the way parents should, and, 
more’s the pity, don’t. It should en¬ 
courage us to develop that spirit of 
comradeship, and we’re willing to do all 
in our power to try . . . but how? 
There are times when counsellors can 
really help campers by talking with 
them, but what is the secret of break¬ 
ing the ice? Please teach us actual 
techniques. 

Now, I realize this is my first year 
at camp. I’m a greenhorn, if you want 
to put it that way. I’m eager to share 
the load, and there’s plenty of work to 
be done. But am I obliged to be a 
Joe Who picks up after everybody else 
and who is at the beck and call of 
anyone who won’t take responsibility 
himself? I don’t like Joe-jobs as a 
steady diet. They should be shared by 
everybody. 


T ronto , Canada , December, 1953 


23 



It seems to me that each camp has 
its share of those who refuse to carry 
their full responsibility programme-wise 
or otherwise. So often when anything 
is to be done it’s a case of “let George 
do it”, and I believe that one point 
could be highlighted and counteracted 
during an in-camp training session for 
all counsellors, new and old. How 
about it? 

And why are salaries not standard¬ 
ized? Why is it that one of my class 
mates who had half my responsibility 
was paid nearly twice as much, and 
another who did far more than I 
iFeceived a smaller salary? Also, why 
must the parents of Counsellors-in- 
Training be asked to pay half fees when 
that G.I.T. is on full-time duty most 
of the day? That boy or girl is learning 
the skill of being a counsellor; he or 
she is giving time and energy all sum¬ 
mer; I believe the summer should be 
free . . . without camp fees, without 
salary. Then when it comes to salary 
time, let there be a set scale: so much 
for the first year, so much for the 
second year and so on, with a bonus 
system, perhaps, for those who deserve 
more. That would save hard feeling, 
and would discourage this business of 
“shopping around” at the beginning of 
the year. 

As far as facilities for counsellors 
are concerned, the concensus seems to 
be that they are pretty fair. The great 
need in some camps, apparently, is a 
counsellor’s haven where they can meet 
every night after the section is settled, 
where they can talk, make coffee, eat 
buns, sing if they want to and not feel 
they must talk in whispers. A counsel¬ 
lor needs this relaxation after a day 
with children if he or she is to mature 
and remain sane for the duration. 


Food is another topic of great 
interest; especially must there be a sub¬ 
stantial snack at bed-time. Most of us 
have worked energetically; we’re really 
ready for another small meal, and 
haven’t the money to spend at the local 
beanery (if there is one within five 
miles) every evening. 

There may be other small details 
which should be covered, but these are 
the chief “beefs”. Possibly another 
G.I.T. or Junior Counsellor will add 
to this in another issue, just to show 
you how our thoughts are running. - 

We love camp, and we want to go 
back. But we want it to be as perfect 
as possible so that we can give campers 
the best that camping has to offer. 


AS CAMP IS 

... to a Counsellor-in-Training 
Anne Davidson, Camp Wahcahmie 

Camp, to me, is life at its fullest. 

It offers relaxation for the mind, 
refreshment for the body, and nourish¬ 
ment for the spirit. My mind becomes 
relaxed when it is transferred from an 
environment which taxes my mental 
powers, to one which lays emphasis on 
refreshing my body. 

Undoubtedly, camping in the true 
sense is to find such refreshment. This 
challenging, invigorating life provides 
me with a salubrious body recreationed 
by various activities: canoeing, swim¬ 
ming, sailing and hiking ... all acces¬ 
sible in any camp environment. 

While my body experiences this 
period of transformation, my spirit is

Camp is true living. I thank God 
for such!

Shall We 


Si nft a Son ft of Camp ? 


Dorothy M. Douglas, Chairman 
Canadian Camp Song Book Committee 


Land of the silver birch, 

Home of the beaver. 

Where still the mighty moose 
Wanders at will. 

Blue lake and rocky shore, 

I will return once more. 

Boom-de-de Boom-de-de, 

Boom de-de Boom Boom, 

Boom de-de Boom Boom, Boom. 

(tone suggesting a tom-tom) 

Do you sing this song at your camp? 
Can you tell us its origin? Do you 
know the other verses—for instance, the 
one about the wigwam, of which there 
are several versions: 

High on a rocky ledge 
PH build my wigwam; 

Close by the water's edge. 

Silent and still. 

Some camps sing “I’ll pitch my wigr 
warn”; others, “I’ll set my wigwam”. 
Some have their wigwam “Close to the 
forest edge”. Now, as good campers, 
what shall we sing? The westerners 
choose to pitch their wigwam, for out 
there the Indian wigwams are usually 
tents of skins or mats. However, certain 
North American Indians live in wig¬ 
wams that are really huts of bark. In 
the interests of helping our campers 
learn to choos^^gqpd camp site, what 
should they glean rk>m singing about 
this wigwam*s*5odation? 


While we are speaking of Indians, 
here is an action song that many camps 
sing, its origin unknown to us. The first 
version we quote from a western camp 
song sheet: 

We are the red men, tall and STRAIGHT, 
In our feathers and war paint. 

Pow-wow, Pow-wow, 

We're the men of the old Hancow . . . 

We CAN fight with sticks and stones 
Bows and arrows, bricks and bones . . . 

the second version comes from an 
eastern one: 

We are the red men, tall and QUAINT, 

In our feathers and war paint, 

Pow-wow, Pow-wow, 

We're the men of the old Duncow . . . 

We DON'T fight with sticks and stones 
Bows and arrows, bricks and bones . . , 

The difference here is quite significant. 
How easily words take a gradual 
change, and sometimes the song will 
create a different image or idea as a 
result. For instance, here is a Canoeing 
Song which someone wrote to a grace¬ 
ful waltz tune. The last two lines of 
one version are: 

And swiftly, as the heron winging, 

Our singing paddles DIP by. 

In the next song sheet we find that the 
paddles zip by, and in yet another they 
slip by. We nearly all sing that jolly 
action song about “My Tall Silk Hat” 
to the tune “Funiculi, Funicula”; but

and help along the work of this c6m- 
mittee? And if you have an extra five 
minutes to spare, would you star those 
songs the campers enjoy particularly, 
and indicate those songs whose words 
and/or music originated at your camp? 
(The committee will ask your permis¬ 
sion before publishing or using these in 
any way). We hope that by the time 
you read this, the committee will be at 
work on the next phase of this under¬ 
taking. 

While reading through the camp 
replies that have come in this fall, it 
has been fun to picture the many 
different camp fires—at the seaside, 
among the mountains, in the prairie 
coulees, by the inland lakes—where this 
past summer, campers and their coun¬ 
sellors sang these songs together, some¬ 
times with jubilant shouts, at other 
times in quiet harmony. Do you re¬ 
member how the C.B.C. conveyed a 
broadcast farewell to the Queen (then 
Princess Elizabeth) and the Duke of 
Edinburgh as they came to the end of 
their tour of Canada? Beginning with 
the first line of Auld Lang Syne in 
Vancouver, the voices of Canadians 
were picked up by the microphone, a 
line or so from each province, until 
the song had been sung through the 
breadth of the Dominion. Travelling 
in imagination from east to west, one 
can hear such songs as Fire’s Burning, 
Taps, and Witchcraft greeting the sun¬ 
set from campfires all across Canada 
on the warm summer evenings. What 
could more naturally express the bond 
between campers from sea to sea than 
the songs we sing together? Surely we 
want such experiences as these to be 
enriched with the heritage of fine and 
vital music—music that belongs with, 
or grows out of, the adventure of camp¬ 
ing in Canada.

\o, Canada , December, 1953 


Standards 

in Ontarii* Camps 

— A Progress Report 
R. Keith Cleverdon 

For over ten years the Ontario 
Camping Association has been studying 
the whole field of camping standards, 
with the eventual aim of helping mem¬ 
ber camps provide a more useful and 
healthful camp experience for the girls 
and boys who attend them. About a 
year ago, a great deal of thought was 
given to a proposal to accredit camps 
belonging to the Association. The 
Standards Committee studied the ques¬ 
tion at some length and recommended 
the adoption of a system for the accred¬ 
iting of camps. This recommendation 
was discussed thoroughly at the annual 
meeting in February, 1953, and 
adopted. 

We feel that camping people across 
Canada will be interested in the next 
step being taken to achieve this goal. 
In June, a survey of member camps 
was conducted by an anonymous ques¬ 
tionnaire. Each camp director was 
asked a number of questions about his 
camp and its operation, designed to see 
if the camp met the standards pro¬ 
posed by the Standards Committee. We 
were very anxious to know if the 
standards we proposed were too severe. 
The results are very interesting. We 
worked out the number of camps com¬ 
plying with each of the various require¬ 
ments, and found the percentage. It 
is significant that the most severe 
requirements are being met by 65% 
of all the Camps, and the most lenient 
by 100% of them. A very large 
proportion of all the camps now satisfy 
all of the minimum standards. Some 
interesting items are these: 100% of 
the camps use pasteurized milk, 77% 
test their water supply every two weeks 
at leasts 63% have hot shower or bath¬ 
tub facilities for all their campers, 90% 


of those without resident doctors have 
one on call, but only 65% insist on pre¬ 
camp medical inspections of staff and 
campers. A daily rest period for camp' 
ers is standard practice in all of the 
camps. In the area of waterfront 
safety, and we believe due largely to 
the efforts of the Canadian Red Cross 
Society, a ve:ry large proportion of the 
camps comply with the standards. 
While only 75% allow not more than 
ten children to one lifeguard, 80% or 
more comply with all the other stand¬ 
ards. The supply of counsellors is 
getting to be a problem with most 
camps, and this was evident from the 
study. In the private camps, 30% used 
17-year old counsellors as a minimum, 
but the average age was not less than 
19 in any camp; agency camps present 
a different picture, with counsellors as 
young as 15 or 16 in one-third of the 
camps, and counsellors-in-training as 
young as 13 in some. The average age 
in agency camps was 17 or more in 
80% of the camps. 

As a result of this survey, the 
Standards Committee of the Ontario 
Camping Association recommended 
that its Proposed Minimum Standards 
be adopted, to replace the Standards 
developed in the 1947-49 period. Since 
these Proposed Standards had been 
circulated to all members in January, 
1953, had been discussed at some length 
at the Conference in February, and 
were apparendy acceptable to most 
camps now, this forward step was 
taken. We would like to stress that 
these standards are not mandatory for 
membership in the Ontario Camping 
Association, though we would like to 
believe that all of our members will 
strive to meet them. Copies of the 
standards will be mailed to all Ontario 
camp directors shortly, and others 
interested in having a set, or in learning 
more of the results of the survey, should 
write to the Association office, 236 
Bloor St. W., Toronto.

Canadian Camping 


hat Camp Means to Me 


Stewart, Director, 
1 W ahcahmie 


A Camp Director 


Those of you who have been in the 
of camping for many years might 
why one who is new to the 
ibouid attempt to expound on such 
ct. I, realize it would be pre- 
uous to make sweeping sugges- 
conceming camping as I feel it 
be, but if one takes a realistic 
one cannot help asking the ques- 
Is camping successful in doing for 
lividual camper all it should? 

ip means certain things in my 
just as it does in the minds of all 
. Ultimately, my camp presents 
:nge, for I see in it an oppor- 
to direct my energies into worth- 
channels. In my hands are the 
ents that may be used success- 
to guide and mould teen-agers. I 
the enormity of this project 
the teen-age personality has 
an intricate but interesting com- 
[-sphere, interesting because it 
a continual dynamic state striving 
rt itself in the enthusiasm and 
ir of everyday living. 

in any other venture, I feel it is 
Bary to have a set of aims which 
^erve as a guide post for me as I 
nff along the camping trail. My 
have become my camp aims . . . 

perhaps, but in their simplicity, 
appear as golden ideas: 

Fo realize beauty in the out-of- 
" is the first aim I endeavour to 
to my campers. Endless opportuni- 
are given to us, as camp directors, 
them that beauty is everywhere, 
have but to attune themselves to 
are to find it; beauty as expressed 


in the silent lapping of waters on the 
shore when all the world is in darkness, 
beauty in the strong purpose of the 
pine as it keeps its lonely vigil on a 
rugged rock; beauty in the fragile 
Indian Pipe, and beauty in the many- 
faceted pebbles among grains of white 
sand. We hope that each camper 
eventually will glory in the fresh and 
unspoiled splendour of the out-of-doors. 

Secondly, my staff and I strive to 
teach our campers the true worth and 
satisfaction that comes from living 
happily with others. The camp en¬ 
vironment is an excellent medium for 
attaining such a satisfaction. Camp 
friends are precious additions to a 
camper’s life, for they share her hours, 
her needs, and her pleasures. She can 
work and play and laugh and sleep 
under the stars in close companionship 
with new-found friends. At camp, she 
is given a lesson in group living, an 
important ingredient in character make¬ 
up. 

The last aim, to me, is all-important 
in that camp seeks to revive the mind 
and body of each camper, so that she 
will return home enriched in spirit, 
eager to recommence study, while the 
memory of her experiences and their 
value will remain with her through life. 
I like to think that a camper’s journey 
through the camp hours will open many 
doors for her . . . doors leading to new 
and varied skills and experiences. 
Whether she has obtained the greatest 
measure from these experiences is 
entirely up to her. In the final reckon¬ 
ing, we, at camp, fervently hope that 
the camper will direct the knowledge

and impressions she has garnered at 
camp into making her a more exciting 
personality. This end may be achieved 
if the camper uses the three aims as 
the steel frame of her compass. 

I truly believe that the most impor¬ 
tant and fascinating ingredient in the 
camp is, undoubtedly, the camper. If 
given the proper guidance, a camper’s 
potentialities can be awakened and 
broadened, fundamentally allowing her 
to blossom into a keener individual. 
You are all interested in the character¬ 
building of each camper . . . for, as 
Baldwin Brown puts it: “Temperament 
we are bom with, character we have to 
make”. Fortunate are we if, through 
camp associations, our energies can be 
directed whole-heartedly into showing 
the camper the way to a richer per¬ 
sonality. Yes! the camper is the main¬ 
spring of camp living. 

As camp directors, we must be ever 
mindful that the capacity to enjoy life 
is recognized as one of the essential 
developments of the individual which 
should come through education. Camp 
should contribute directly to this out¬ 
come. Camp works in the present. It 
is decidedly realistic to the camper. It? 
produces tangible results in success and 
failure. Camp offers opportunities for 
group enterprise which bring the satis¬ 
factions that come from group achieve¬ 
ments. 

May I, at this point, interject a few 
ideas that have occurred to me during 
the year? It is all well and good to say 
that the camper is the mainspring of 
the camp. Naturally enough, without 
campers there would be no camps. 
With this in mind, I would again ask 
the question: How many directors 
believe that camping is doing all it 
should for campers? Do we allow them 
to breathe the true camping air or do 
we smother them with so much instruc¬ 
tion, guidance and observation that they 
have no free time in which to explore 
hidden beauties, to experiment and find 
the best way to do a given task, to 
wander wherever the spirit moves? 

Canajman Camping 






Arc we sure that our counsellors are 
the best to be procured? Each coun¬ 
sellor must be a friend and adviser. 
Do we consider this when we assemble 
cox staff together? What are your 
requirements for a good counsellor? 
I know some directors who consider age 
to be the prime requisite, others who 
advertise that their counsellors are all 
University students, and so on. Might 
oot an eighteen-year-old be just as 
«ootionally mature as a twenty-two- 
old University graduate? Perhaps 
-ces. Perhaps no. But since the material 
w have to work with is so pliable and 
=pressionable, it stands to reason that 
ccr staff should be well screened. 

Do we plan our programme with the 
k5sa in mind that it is what the 
campers so desire, or is it based on the 
activities in which our counsellors are 
most skilled! We put at the campers’ 
disposal recreation which is familiar to 
dadr city life. Should we not expend 


our energies on opening for them 
worlds which afe not accessible during 
the long months away from camp? 
Here is a golden opportunity to present 
experiences . . . everlasting gifts which 
will mould and enlarge their characters. 
Would that more camps concerned 
themselves with the thrills found in 
campcraft and nature lore, in orient¬ 
eering, in archery, in sailing, in water 
skiing, in oil painting; activities carried 
on in the out-of-doors amidst all the 
beauties of nature. 

All campers should experience the 
thrill of canoe-tripping. Poor is the r 
camper who has not tasted the satisfac¬ 
tion which comes from such adventur¬ 
ing. Forever locked in my memory will 
be the fun, fellowship and friends I 
have garnered through the years of 
cooking over a roaring fire, sleeping 
out, paddling through rain and sun¬ 
shine, plotting our way, with compass 
and map as our only guides. In such

Canadian Camping 




Convention 
ISews and Notes 

MEET US IN NEW YORK! 

From where we sit, it looks like a 
Clan Gatherin’ of OCA and GCA 
people next February 2, 3, 4, 5, & 6, 
at the Twenty-third National Conven¬ 
tion of the American Camping Associa¬ 
tion in that glamorous town. Great! 
We can think of no finer way to renew 
friendships and to meet the American 
camping fraternity. - 

Programme takes interesting form as 
United Nations speakers and United 
Nations tours are included in the roster 
of attractions. For instance, a meeting 
in one of the UN Assembly Halls has 
been scheduled for ACA delegates, 
while three UN tours have been 
arranged for those unable to attend the 
Wednesday afternoon meeting. 

Dr. Buel Gallagher, President of City 
College of New York, and former assist¬ 
ant in United States Department of 
Education, gives the opening address on 
Wednesday evening. From Washington 
comes another speaker, Dr. Leland 
Bradford, Director of the National 
Training Laboratory in Group Develop¬ 
ment. 

That’s all we can give you of a 
definite nature to this moment, but pre¬ 
programmes will be ready when this 
magazine is in your hands. Merely 
write to Herman Barr, Programme 
Director, New York Section of the 
American Camping Association, 342 
Madison Avenue, New York City. 

It promises to be a fine show, full of 
the sort of new information we, as 
camping people, require if we are to 
operate at a forward-looking level. 

FOLLOWING THAT . . . 

. . . comes "our own Ontario Camping 
Association Conference at the end of 
February—25, 26 and 27, to be exact 
—in Toronto. Place has been set as 


Central YMCA, 40 College Street, and 
the committee has been working like 
mad since before the summer! 

We think one of the keenest attrac¬ 
tions will be group luncheons which 
are being arranged for those who would 
like them. For instance, the committee 
feels that YMCA camping people, Girl 
Guides, Boy Scouts, Church .camping 
folk, have little time at our pow-wow 
to get together for discussion of their 
own pressing problems. Same goes for 
the directors of boys’ private camps, 
girls’ private camps and co-educational 
private camps. So the luncheon periods 
will be left open on Friday and Satur¬ 
day for just this purpose. Banquets 
with special speakers will be scheduled 
for Friday night and Saturday-night. 

The Programme committee is up to 
its ears in correspondence with special 
speakers for forums, workshops and 
dinners: So, more of that later. 

INTERESTED IN 
FOOD MANAGEMENT? 

When it comes to camp planning, 
every director should want to take 
advantage of a course offered by Ryer- 
son Institute in Toronto; but, believe 
it, there were not enough registrants 
to warrant it this past fall. 

So how about next year? Would 
you be willing to submit your name, 
and show that you would like to be 
included in future classes? If so, one of 
our committee members will see if 
Ryerson Institute will make the same 
offer again. 

Cost of the course was to be $15, 
with classes once a week from October 
to March, covering menu planning, 
food purchasing and general manage¬ 
ment of this department. 

Get in touch with OCA office, 236 
Bloor Street'West; KI. 0151, by letter 
or telephone. If we gather in enough 
names, we’ll take up the matter with 
the Ryerson people.
